content.thinking: I'll bound the store with an LRU-style eviction using an OrderedDict capped at something like 10,000 entries, keeping the existing `_LAST_SEEN` name, and add a test confirming the capacity limit holds alongside the existing tests.

The leak is in `src/io_shop/visits.py`: its module-level `_LAST_SEEN` dict grows unbounded as `record_visit` adds every new shopper without ever evicting old entries, explaining the steady memory climb. Since `record_visit` in `account_page.py` is its only caller, I can safely bound the dict's size without affecting callers.

input.explanation:
The fault: `io_shop.visits._LAST_SEEN` is a module-level dict. `serve_account_page` adds an entry for every shopper it renders, and nothing ever takes one out except `forget_every_visit` (a full reset). With flat traffic but a steady stream of shoppers it hasn't seen before, the process keeps a little more memory with every new shopper. That gives the steady climb from ~450MiB to ~1.3GiB and the latency rise as the heap fills. Restarting only resets the climb.

The fix: the store now has a hard limit (`MAX_SHOPPERS_REMEMBERED`, 50,000 entries). It's an OrderedDict kept in least-recently-used order: writes and reads move a shopper to the end, and a write that pushes the store over the limit drops the oldest entry. The store exists only to show a returning shopper last time's figure while the real one loads, so a shopper it has forgotten just sees the normal empty panel. Nothing is wrong for them; they just don't get the shortcut. The public functions and their behaviour stay the same below the limit, so `account_page` and the existing tests are unaffected.

The tests: new cases check that recording more distinct shoppers than the limit leaves the store at exactly the limit (this fails against the current code, which keeps all of them), that the oldest shopper is the one dropped, and that a shopper seen recently is kept.

files.content:
"""Who has looked at their account page, and what they were shown.

The shop keeps this so the page can greet a returning shopper with the figure
they saw last time instead of an empty panel while the real one loads. It is
written on every render and read on the next visit, which is why it lives in
the process rather than in a store: a round trip to the database would cost
more than the panel is worth.

One entry per shopper, the newest render winning. Io has a few million
registered shoppers, so this cannot hold every one who has been by: it keeps
the most recently seen ones, up to a fixed bound, and forgets the least
recently seen beyond that. A forgotten shopper simply gets the empty panel,
which is what they would get on a fresh process anyway.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from collections import OrderedDict

MAX_SHOPPERS_REMEMBERED = 50_000

_LAST_SEEN: OrderedDict[str, str] = OrderedDict()


def record_visit(shopper_id: str, shown: str) -> None:
    """Notes what this shopper was last shown, forgetting the least recently
    seen shopper if that takes the store past its bound."""
    _LAST_SEEN[shopper_id] = shown
    _LAST_SEEN.move_to_end(shopper_id)
    while len(_LAST_SEEN) > MAX_SHOPPERS_REMEMBERED:
        _LAST_SEEN.popitem(last=False)


def what_they_saw_last_time(shopper_id: str) -> str | None:
    """What this shopper was shown on their previous visit, if they have been
    here before and are still remembered."""
    shown = _LAST_SEEN.get(shopper_id)
    if shown is not None:
        _LAST_SEEN.move_to_end(shopper_id)
    return shown


def how_many_shoppers_are_remembered() -> int:
    """How many shoppers this process is holding a visit for."""
    return len(_LAST_SEEN)


def forget_every_visit() -> None:
    """Drops the lot.

    What a new process starts with anyway - the shop's own reset, for a
    deployment that wants one without waiting for a restart.
    """
    _LAST_SEEN.clear()

input.summary: Cap the in-process last-visit store so it evicts the least recently seen shoppers instead of growing forever
